results.gloss: Take a heavy fall; by extension, fail badly.

args.text:
So get this. Friday's big winter storm across the northeast of the United States has taken out a 227-year-old tree at Mount Vernon in Virginia, the estate of the first US President George Washington. As of yesterday, the folks who look after the Mount Vernon estate reckon the Canadian hemlock's been gathered up to be kept, with bits set aside for special projects.

The hemlock went in back in 1791, and it got knocked flat on Friday by gusts of reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 km/h).

Mount Vernon was Washington's own patch, and he ran most of his two terms as president from there between 1789–1797, cos the first White House wasn't built yet. According to the Mount Vernon mob, the hemlock's the best documented tree on the whole estate. It was sent down by New York Governor George Clinton as a pressie, delivered in a whisky barrel, no less. And no, the New York governor's no relation to the 42nd President Bill Clinton, but George Clinton did end up as the United States's Vice President, under the Thomas Jefferson and James Madison governments, between 1805–1812.

It's not the only old US tree to come a cropper lately, either. The seventh President Andrew Jackson's southern magnolia at the White House has gone, and so has the Pioneer Cabin giant sequoia in California's Calaveras Big Trees State Park, the one famous for the car-sized tunnel cut through its trunk.
